title: Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.
lead: Two subcontractors completed their work, but the general contractor invoked language tying final payment to payment by an owner in bankruptcy.

actors.name: Peacock Construction Co.
actors.role: General contractor withholding final subcontract payments

actors.name: Modern Air Conditioning and Overly Manufacturing
actors.role: Subcontractors who completed the air-conditioning and rooftop-pool work

proceedings: Separate circuit-court summary judgments favored the subcontractors.
Florida Supreme Court adopted those decisions and discharged certiorari, leaving the judgments intact.
limits: The decision construes ambiguous final-payment provisions, preserving clearly expressed risk shifting. It neither fixes a new precise due date nor decides every contractual ambiguity.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: The project’s owner does not pay in full
paragraphs: Peacock was general contractor on a condominium project. Modern Air Conditioning undertook heating and air conditioning; Overly Manufacturing undertook the rooftop swimming pool. Each subcontract placed final payment within thirty days after completion, written architectural acceptance, and full owner payment.

Both completed their work and requested payment. No deficiencies had been found. Modern’s architect testified that its equipment, although not yet operated, was complete under the plans and specifications. The owner, a corporation, entered bankruptcy, and Peacock had not received full payment. Peacock’s position made interpretation decisive: did owner payment condition any debt, or merely fix timing for an otherwise unconditional obligation?

sections.title: Both subcontractors obtain summary judgment
sections.cue: A conflict concerns whether intent must go to a jury
paragraphs: Modern and Overly sued separately in Lee County Circuit Court and each won summary judgment. The Second District affirmed Modern under the prevailing approach treating such clauses as absolute payment promises with reasonable timing, then affirmed Overly on Modern’s authority.

The Florida Supreme Court accepted conflict certiorari and consolidated the causes for appellate purposes. In Gerrits, the Third District had reversed a similar subcontractor judgment because intent should go to a jury when the contractor raised it. Peacock conceded the weight of contrary authority but sought an opportunity to present intent evidence before any directed verdict.

sections.title: The familiar commercial relationship resolves the ambiguity
sections.cue: Clear language can allocate a different risk
paragraphs: Acting Chief Justice Boyd acknowledged that the language could describe either a condition or reasonable payment timing. The court did not pretend Peacock’s reading was linguistically impossible. It held that judicial interpretation could resolve ordinary intent in this familiar transaction without a mandatory jury trial merely because the text was ambiguous.

Small subcontractors on large projects ordinarily need payment to remain in business and do not intend to insure the owner’s solvency. The court therefore read ambiguous owner-payment clauses as unconditional promises payable within a reasonable time. Listing owner receipt alongside completion and acceptance did not itself transfer permanent nonpayment risk.
Parties remained free to shift that risk, but had to express the shift unambiguously, with the general contractor bearing the burden of clear expression. These subcontracts did not do so.

sections.title: The subcontractor judgments remain in effect
sections.cue: The conflicting precedent is displaced to that extent
paragraphs: On December 15, 1977, the Supreme Court adopted the Second District’s decisions as controlling Florida law, overruled Gerrits insofar as inconsistent, and discharged the certiorari orders. Both favorable summary judgments remained undisturbed and did not depend on the bankrupt owner eventually paying Peacock. Justices England, Sundberg, Hatchett, and Karl joined Boyd without a separate opinion.
